definition: Stringent means strict and tightly binding — said of rules, standards, and requirements that leave little slack and demand real effort to satisfy.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word stringent. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know stringent should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Visa rules for the fellowship were stringent: original documents only, four proofs of residence, and a filing window nine days wide.
Firm is milder than stringent: a firm rule holds steady and expects compliance, while a stringent one binds tight — exacting, detailed, and costly to satisfy.
Draconian is harsher than stringent: stringent standards are demanding but defensible, while draconian ones are so severe that they read as punishment rather than rigor.

Stringent lives up to its root: the requirements bind tight.
Notice what carries the word — standards, rules, limits.
The inspectors enforcing them may be strict or even harsh, but stringent belongs to the requirements themselves.
Stringent is the auditor's adjective: it attaches to codes, standards, deadlines, and requirements, and it certifies that they bind tight.
Keep people out of its reach — a demanding teacher is strict, not stringent — and keep your grip on the spelling: astringent, its cousin, is a different word for a different job.
Between lax and draconian, stringent marks the tight-but-defensible stretch of how hard a rule can press.
